report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is only partly supported. CLA supplements may produce a *small* reduction in body fat in some adults, but evidence that they reliably reduce **abdominal/visceral fat** is limited and not strong enough to make CLA a dependable treatment.

**Evidence supporting the view:** A small randomized trial in obese men with metabolic syndrome reported reduced abdominal adipose tissue after four weeks of CLA, but found no accompanying improvement in overall obesity or other cardiovascular-risk measures; the authors explicitly noted the limited sample size. Another six-month placebo-controlled trial in 40 healthy overweight adults reported reduced body fat and less holiday weight gain.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16924272/

**Why confidence should be modest:** CLA studies differ substantially in dose, duration, participant health, the CLA-isomer mix, and whether “abdominal fat” was directly measured versus inferred from waist circumference. Human results have been inconsistent, unlike the much larger effects seen in animals. A recent systematic review/meta-analysis assessed body mass, BMI, waist circumference, fat mass, body-fat percentage, and fat-free mass across randomized trials—appropriate evidence for the question—but the existence of this broad, heterogeneous literature does not establish a large or clinically meaningful abdominal-fat effect for an individual supplement user.  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366

CLA is not risk-free: formulations and isomers matter, and clinical resources note uncertain human benefit and potential metabolic concerns. Discuss it with a clinician, particularly with diabetes, liver disease, or lipid abnormalities.
